item.title: Bids sought for hospital project
item.description: The India-funded 100-bed super-specialty hospital project in Fiji is moving closer to construction with shortlisted companies set to arrive this month for site assessments as preparations continue for a groundbreaking early next year. Indian High Commissioner to Fiji Suneet Mehta said the project was progressing well with the tendering process underway for what will be India’s largest grant assist
item.content:encoded:
The India-funded 100-bed super-specialty hospital project in Fiji is moving closer to construction with shortlisted companies set to arrive this month for site assessments as preparations continue for a groundbreaking early next year.

Indian High Commissioner to Fiji Suneet Mehta said the project was progressing well with the tendering process underway for what will be India’s largest grant assistance project in the Pacific region.

He said shortlisted companies would visit Fiji to assess the site, understand the requirements and engage with relevant stakeholders before submitting their bids.

“We expect the team of shortlisted companies to come over to Fiji to do a site visit, understand the lay of the land, interact with all the relevant stakeholders over here,” Mr Mehta said.

He said the visits would help companies prepare their bids, with the selection process expected to move forward soon to allow preparations for the groundbreaking.

“We will hopefully shortlist a bidder soon so that they can start preparations for the groundbreaking to be held by early next year.”

The hospital will be built in Nasinu on land already earmarked for the project and is expected to strengthen Fiji’s healthcare infrastructure.

Mr Mehta said the facility would bring expertise from India through doctors, nurses, equipment and medicines to provide world-class healthcare services in Fiji.

item.title: Hibiscus hopefuls unveiled
item.description: TWELVE women have been unveiled as contestants for the 2026 FMF Hibiscus Festival, marking the beginning of this year’s journey toward the festival crown. The contestants include students, youth leaders, advocates, a journalist and a medical imaging student, each bringing their own experiences and community causes to the annual festival.
item.content:encoded:
TWELVE women have been unveiled as contestants for the 2026 FMF Hibiscus Festival, marking the beginning of this year’s journey toward the festival crown.

The contestants include students, youth leaders, advocates, a journalist and a medical imaging student, each bringing their own experiences and community causes to the annual festival.

Among them are Bulou Boteiova, a Yasawa-born educator and former Miss Coral Coast; Olivia Luisa Gade, a vibrant and faith-driven young professional; Kali Maria Shaw, a medical student promoting health awareness; and Leona Douglas, a political science student advocating for women’s health and youth development.

Also joining the lineup are Temalesi Vakalawa Alutakua, a youth leader focused on mental health support; Nicole Matavesi, Fiji’s Youth Prime Minister; Keren Koroi, a mental health advocate; and Potaisia Rokowailoa, a medical imaging student who champions inclusive communities and challenges stigma through collective support.

Completing the field are journalist Suliana Elizabeth Latianara, youth advocate Sala Korosaya, environmental advocate Salanieta Sekiseki and Emi Ravela, a law student passionate about women’s empowerment and girls’ education.

The 12 contestants will now begin their FMF Hibiscus Festival journey, representing a wide range of professions, experiences and causes while competing for the 2026 Hibiscus crown.

item.title: Ban review every 6 months
item.description: THE ban on the movement of fresh produce from the Yasawa and Mamanuca groups is reviewed every six months, says Commissioner Western Apolosi Lewaqai. Authorities are working with the Biosecurity Authority of Fiji (BAF), Ministry of Agriculture, Fiji Police Force and maritime operators to enforce the restrictions through inspections, public awareness and monitoring, Mr Lewaqai said.
item.content:encoded:
THE ban on the movement of fresh produce from the Yasawa and Mamanuca groups is reviewed every six months, says Commissioner Western Apolosi Lewaqai.

Authorities are working with the Biosecurity Authority of Fiji (BAF), Ministry of Agriculture, Fiji Police Force and maritime operators to enforce the restrictions through inspections, public awareness and monitoring, Mr Lewaqai said.

Yesterday, BAF warned that anyone caught breaching the ban could face a $1000 fine.

The restrictions remain in place to contain the Tongan fruit fly, with the movement of host fruits and vegetables from the Yasawa and Mamanuca groups strictly prohibited.

Meanwhile, the ban has had little impact on fruit and vegetable supplies at the Lautoka market.

Lautoka Market Vendors Association president Filomena O’Neil said most produce sold at the market came from the interior rather than the islands.

item.title: Family hospitalised after fish poisoning
item.description: A FAMILY in Nabua, Suva, was hospitalised after suffering suspected fish poisoning following a Sunday lunch of Ogo. Ruci Cika said several members of her household developed severe symptoms within hours of eating the fish she had prepared.
item.content:encoded:
A FAMILY in Nabua, Suva, was hospitalised after suffering suspected fish poisoning following a Sunday lunch of Ogo.

Ruci Cika said several members of her household developed severe symptoms within hours of eating the fish she had prepared.

“After we ate, around 2 to 3pm, our stomachs started to hurt, including the children. We were vomiting and constantly going to the toilet.”

She said her daughter was among the first to become seriously ill.

“One of my daughters was rushed to CWM Hospital as her case was very serious. After half an hour, I also became very weak in my body, the same with my grandchildren, so all went to the CWM Hospital.”

Ms Cika said other family members later became ill and were taken to the hospital, including her husband.

She said everyone who ate the fish was admitted.

Several other individuals have reported cases of fish poisoning but Assistant Minister for Health Penioni Ravunawa said the ministry was not aware of any reported fish poisoning cases.

He said any verified information would be shared through the ministry’s media channels.

Questions sent to the Ministry of Fisheries remained unanswered.

item.title: Tui Nayau calls for fairness
item.description: TUI Nayau Ratu Tevita Uluilakeba Mara has called for fairness from Government over the distribution of funding to rural and maritime communities. Following an official five-day visit to Australia where he met with his kinsmen, Ratu Tevita noted how many of their conversations focused on the government funded developments in communities across the country.
item.content:encoded:
TUI Nayau Ratu Tevita Uluilakeba Mara has called for fairness from Government over the distribution of funding to rural and maritime communities.

Following an official five-day visit to Australia where he met with his kinsmen, Ratu Tevita noted how many of their conversations focused on the government funded developments in communities across the country.

He said while he welcomed and supported the construction of new roads built in Vanua Levu and Taveuni, there was a need to also focus on other maritime communities.

“There are islands in my province where a mother carrying a baby must be handed out of a small boat into the swell, because there is nowhere to land – Nayau, Moce, Kabara, Ono-i-Lau, Fulaga.

“I could name more. We are not asking for anything grand. We are asking for somewhere to put our feet down.”

The Tui Nayau, however, maintained their concern does not take away the equally important needs of other communities.

“And let no one hear this as one province speaking against another. Lau wants nothing that belongs to Vanua Levu, or to Kadavu, or Rotuma, or the villages in the highlands of Viti Levu, or the settlements of the cane belt. Their case is ours. This country is not a small table with too many hands reaching for it. We are one people — iTaukei, Indo-Fijian, Rotuman, and everyone else who calls these islands home and a nation is measured by how it treats those who live furthest from its capital.”

He said the province, while small, had contributed immensely to Fiji’s economy.

“I am told sometimes that money spent in Lau does not return.

“Fiji’s economy is not held up only in the places where the money is made. It is held up by people from those small islands who run businesses in Suva, Lautoka and Labasa, who teach in our schools and nurse in our hospitals, who serve in the Force and in the church – and by our sons and daughters overseas, in the very places I have just come from, whose remittances have carried this country through every hard year it has had.”

item.title: Speaker stresses gender diversity
item.description: THE question of increasing the number of women in Parliament is not simply about gender equality but about strengthening democracy, governance and national development. Speaker of Parliament Filimone Jitoko said this at the opening the 14th Speaker’s Debate in Suva on Thursday evening as he challenged participants to look beyond women’s participation in politics and focus on increasing their repre
item.content:encoded:
THE question of increasing the number of women in Parliament is not simply about gender equality but about strengthening democracy, governance and national development.

Speaker of Parliament Filimone Jitoko said this at the opening the 14th Speaker’s Debate in Suva on Thursday evening as he challenged participants to look beyond women’s participation in politics and focus on increasing their representation in decision-making roles.

“To put it very simply, the question of women’s representation in politics is not merely a women’s issue,” he said.

“It is a democratic issue, it is a governance issue, it is a national development issue and above all, it’s a human rights issue.”

Speaking on the theme “From Participation to Representation: How Do We Increase Women in Parliament?”, Mr Jitoko said participation referred to citizens engaging in political life through activities such as voting, protesting or attending public discussions, while representation meant serving as decision-makers in Parliament or local government.

“So, this theme invites us all to look beyond the aspirations through participatory engagement to action as a decision-maker.”

Mr Jitoko said diverse decision-making bodies strengthened democratic legitimacy, enriched public debate and improved policy outcomes.

He noted that Fiji currently had only five women serving as members of Parliament despite many qualified women being available to serve.

“Their relatively small number reminds us all that there is still considerable distance to travel before representation more closely reflects the population we serve.”

Mr Jitoko said creating greater opportunities for women to enter politics would ultimately strengthen Fiji’s democratic institutions and ensure all citizens had an equal opportunity to contribute to national decision-making.

item.title: Hope for side visit to Tuvalu
item.description: THE Pacific’s fight against rising sea levels will be brought closer to world leaders through a proposed visit to Tuvalu during the pre-COP conference in Nadi. Fiji is hoping more world leaders will attend the conference and have the opportunity to see first-hand the impact of climate change on Pacific Island countries.
item.content:encoded:
THE Pacific’s fight against rising sea levels will be brought closer to world leaders through a proposed visit to Tuvalu during the pre-COP conference in Nadi.

Fiji is hoping more world leaders will attend the conference and have the opportunity to see first-hand the impact of climate change on Pacific Island countries.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka said leaders would have an opportunity to travel to Tuvalu to witness the effects of rising sea levels before returning to Fiji.

“We were hoping that more world leaders will come to Fiji for the pre-COP conference,” he said.

Mr Rabuka said Fiji had asked Australia to support hosting the pre-COP conference in the Pacific before the main event in Turkey.

“It will be an opportunity for them to go out and see for themselves what is happening in some of the islands that have been badly affected by climate change, particularly in Tuvalu.”

However, he said some leaders would not be able to attend because of other priorities.

“Unfortunately, some of the leaders will not be able to come, and I don’t blame them. They probably have higher priorities.”

He said the Pacific needed more leaders to attend so they could better understand the region’s concerns.

“Those of us right in the front line of the brunt of climate change.

“We are hoping more of them would come, so that when we go and present our case to them, they’d be able to understand well.”

The pre-COP meeting is expected to provide an important platform for Pacific nations to highlight the impacts of climate change.

item.title: Authority issues warning
item.description: SPEEDING, unsafe overtaking, impatience, and poor judgement can turn an ordinary journey into a tragedy in a matter of seconds, stated the Land Transport Authority (LTA). Following the double fatality in Navua on Wednesday, the LTA issued a statement calling for motorists to prioritise road safety first rather than arriving early at a certain destination.
item.content:encoded:
SPEEDING, unsafe overtaking, impatience, and poor judgement can turn an ordinary journey into a tragedy in a matter of seconds, stated the Land Transport Authority (LTA).

Following the double fatality in Navua on Wednesday, the LTA issued a statement calling for motorists to prioritise road safety first rather than arriving early at a certain destination.

“Every road death is a devastating reminder that the decisions we make on the road carry consequences far beyond the moment, no destination is worth risking a life.” the LTA stated.

“While the Land Transport Authority extends its deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the two individuals, who tragically lost their lives on our roads, it is strongly urging every road user to adapt a change in mindset as road users, drivers, cyclists, passengers, pedestrians and to exercise greater care, patience and responsibility on our roads.”

The authority is urging motorists to slow down, maintain a safe distance, and only overtake when it is safe and necessary to do so.

“As passengers, speak up when a driver is taking unnecessary risks. As pedestrians and other road users, remain alert and make safety a shared responsibility, take your time, make the right decision, arrive alive.”

It stressed that road safety is about valuing life and not only about following the road rules.
